summary: Describes why it is useful to move context between nodes in an IP access network when a mobile host changes subnets. Services such as AAA, header compression and QoS would otherwise need to be set up again from scratch after each move.

plainLanguage.summary: When you move to a new classroom, the teacher would have to relearn everything about you. Passing your file along from the old room saves starting over.

questions: why transfer context between access routers
what is the context transfer problem in mobility
how does context transfer reduce handover delays
subtitle: Why mobile hosts need to quickly re-establish network services when moving between subnets.

tldr.problem: When a mobile host moves to a new subnet, it must re-establish services like AAA, header compression, and QoS from scratch, causing delays that harm real-time applications.
tldr.mechanism: Context transfer copies the state of these services from the old network node to the new one, allowing the host to resume service quickly without redoing protocol exchanges.
tldr.outcome: This can significantly reduce handover delays for mobile hosts, making seamless mobility possible for time-sensitive applications like VoIP and video.

today: RFC 3374 is an Informational document that identifies the problem of service re-establishment delays during mobile handovers. The document has not been obsoleted and remains a key motivation for context transfer protocol development in mobile networks.

sections.title: The Handover Problem
sections.content:
Mobile hosts move frequently between network subnets, and when they do, routing must be updated to deliver their traffic to the new point of access. However, the mobile host's connection to the network is controlled by a collection of context transfer-candidate services that were established at the old subnet. These services include Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA), header compression, and Quality of Service (QoS), each one carefully negotiated at the old network node.

If the mobile host must re-establish all of these services from scratch at the new subnet using the same protocol exchanges as before, the process can be very time-consuming. For real-time applications such as VoIP telephony and video, this delay-sensitive traffic can be seriously impacted during the handover.
sections.plainLanguage: When you move to a new place, people have to learn who you are and what you need. That takes time. If someone tells the new people about you first, they're ready for you right away.

sections.title: Services Worth Preserving
sections.content:
Three key services motivate context transfer. Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) establishes whether the host has the right to network access. After successful initial authentication, transferring the AAA context means the mobile host can continue access without redoing the entire authentication exchange with a new AAA server. This is particularly valuable because authentication is computationally expensive and time-consuming.

Header compression is used on low-bandwidth radio links to reduce the size of IP headers sent over the air. Establishing header compression requires multiple exchanges with the new router before full compression becomes available, during which the host experiences reduced application bandwidth. If the compression context is transferred, full compression can be available immediately.

Quality of Service (QoS) mechanisms ensure that the host's traffic receives appropriate forwarding treatment in the network. Preliminary studies show that re-establishing QoS from scratch can be very time-consuming for mobile handovers, making context transfer valuable for maintaining adequate application performance.
sections.plainLanguage: Your school knows you are allowed to be there, you speak English, and you get special help with math. A new school would have to check all of that again. If your old school sends a note, the new school skips the checking.

sections.title: Why a Common Solution Matters
sections.content:
Different Layer 2 radio protocols may define their own context transfer solutions. Organizations like 3GPP and IEEE are working on such solutions, which are optimized for specific radio access technologies. However, if different radio protocols use different context transfer mechanisms, a mobile host moving between technologies (for example, from Wi-Fi to cellular) would face a significant problem: either a gateway would be required to translate between mechanisms, or the host would have to perform a full re-initialization of services from scratch.

A common Layer 3 context transfer solution at the IP level would work across any Layer 2 radio access technology, enabling seamless mobility for hosts with multiple radio interfaces. This interoperability is the second major motivation for context transfer.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine your school uses one filing system but the next school uses a different one. If the governments agreed on a common way to send files, any school could talk to any other school.

sections.title: When Context Transfer May Not Help
sections.content:
Context transfer is not always the best solution. Router compatibility is a practical concern: context transfer between two routers is only possible if the receiving router supports the same services as the sending router. A router that cannot use received context should simply refuse the transfer, which results in the same situation as a handover without context transfer.

In some cases, mobile hosts or access networks may prefer to re-negotiate the level of service when crossing administrative domain boundaries, where policies differ. Context transfer assumes that quickly re-establishing the same service level is desirable, but this may not always be true.

For certain types of service, such as multicast or push information services, context transfer may not be faster than establishing from scratch. Additionally, when both subnets support the same Layer 2 radio access technology with their own Layer 2 handover mechanisms, Layer 3 context transfer may not provide significant improvement over those existing Layer 2 solutions.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the new teacher does not want your file. Sometimes you cross into a country with different rules and have to start over. Sometimes it is faster to just ask the new teacher to check you out than to have someone read your file.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
Context transfer introduces security challenges. The context may contain sensitive information that users or operators want to keep hidden from unauthorized viewers, so the transfer process must protect information privacy. Transfer legitimacy is critical: a false or corrupted context transfer could severely impact the receiving router and the access network, enabling denial-of-service or theft-of-service attacks.

Some context may include security association information pertinent to encryption keys or authentication credentials established between the mobile host and other network entities. This security context must be preserved during handover with appropriate security measures.

A key concern: context transfer requires a trust relationship between network entities. If one router is compromised and transfers corrupted security context to a new router, the security of the whole system can be reduced. The compromised context may be used to decrypt communication channels. When context transfer is not used, compromise of one router only affects what that router can see, and security can be re-established at a new entity.
sections.plainLanguage: Your school file might say your parents' phone number and what medicines you take. A bad person could steal that if they read the file. The old school has to be really careful when sending it.

sections.title: Next Steps
sections.content:
The RFC recommends that the Seamoby Working Group investigate two key areas. First, identify candidate router-related services for context transfer and analyze the transfer requirements for each one. This analysis should determine which services benefit most from context transfer and which services face practical limitations.

Second, develop a framework and protocol(s) that will support the transfer of context between the routing nodes of an IP network. Any context transfer solution must inter-work with existing and emerging IP protocols, in particular those protocols supporting mobility in an IP network such as Mobile IPv4 and Mobile IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: The next step is for experts to agree on which information is worth sending and how to send it safely.
